## Start with your question

The package provides 40 statistical functions and a searchable method catalog.
Choose a statistical procedure based on the quantity you want to estimate
and your study design. A sample mean, a proportion, and a
median answer different questions. A paired comparison needs matched observations.
The package does not automatically select a valid method for your data.

| Your question | Function |
|---|---|
| What do these observations look like? | `describe_numeric()` |
| What is the population mean? | `mean_t_ci()` or `bootstrap_mean_ci()` |
| What proportion of trials succeed? | `proportion_ci()` |
| What is the population median? | `median_ci()` |
| How do independent group means differ? | `mean_difference_ci()` |
| How do matched observations differ? | `paired_mean_ci()` |
| How are two variables associated? | `correlation_estimate()` or `correlation_ci()` |
| How does a response relate to predictors? | `ols_fit()` |
| How many observations should I plan? | `sample_size_mean()` |

## Find a statistical method

Use `bambagana_catalog()` to explore available methods.
Search by a statistical topic, function name, or description.
The catalog helps locate functions; it does not select
a statistically valid method for a particular dataset.

```{r}
library(bambaganaCI)
bambagana_catalog("confidence")
bambagana_catalog("regression")
```

For an individual method, consult its help page to review
the arguments, assumptions, and returned results.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?mean_t_ci
```

## Load the package and describe your data

Replace these illustrative scores with your own independent observations.
No packages are installed by this vignette.

```{r}
set.seed(1998)
scores <- c(8, 10, 12, 9, 15, 11, 13, 10, 14, 12)
describe_numeric(scores)
```

The mean summarizes the ordinary average; the standard deviation describes
variation between observations. The standard error of the mean describes
uncertainty in the estimated mean. These are different quantities.

```{r}
mean_se(scores)
mean_t_ci(scores)
```

The t interval has exact coverage under independent normal sampling with common
positive variance. Outside that model it is approximate. It estimates the
population mean, not the range containing 95% of individual observations.

A percentile bootstrap interval resamples the observed scores. It is an
alternative construction with its own coverage limitations, especially for
small, skewed or heavy-tailed samples.

```{r}
set.seed(1998)
bootstrap_mean_ci(scores, B = 2000, method = "percentile")
```

## Estimate a proportion

Suppose 40 of 100 independent trials were successes.

```{r}
p <- proportion_ci(successes = 40, trials = 100, method = "wilson")
p
```

The estimate is 40%. The interval describes uncertainty about the common
population success probability. Its coverage is approximate. Selecting
`method = "exact"` uses a conservative exact binomial interval instead.
Neither choice fixes dependence between trials or biased sampling.

The displayed percentages leave the stored values on their original 0-to-1 scale.

```{r}
p$estimate
coef(p)
confint(p)
as.data.frame(p)
```

The table is suitable for saving or combining. `confint()` only extracts existing
limits. To change the level, recalculate with `conf = 0.90`; relabeling an existing
95% interval as 90% would be incorrect.

```{r}
proportion_ci(40, 100, conf = 0.90)
```

## Compare two independent groups

These illustrative measurements represent separate, independent groups.

```{r}
group1 <- c(8, 10, 12, 9, 15, 11, 13, 10, 14, 12)
group2 <- c(10, 12, 14, 13, 16, 14, 11, 15, 13, 12)
comparison <- mean_difference_ci(group1, group2)
comparison
```

The difference is **group 1 minus group 2**. A negative estimate means group 1's
sample mean is smaller. The default is Welch inference. Use paired methods only
when observations are actually matched; equal sample sizes alone do not make
observations paired. A confidence interval including zero does not establish
that the two population means are identical.

## Test a statistical claim

Confidence intervals estimate an unknown population quantity.
Hypothesis tests assess a specified claim about that quantity.
The choice of test depends on the study design and assumptions.

### Test a population mean

Suppose the question is whether the population mean score
differs from 10. The null hypothesis states that the mean
equals 10; the alternative states that it differs from 10.

```{r}
mean_test(scores, mu = 10)
```

The p-value measures how unusual the observed test statistic
would be, under the null hypothesis and the test assumptions.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A small p-value provides evidence against the stated null
hypothesis; it does not measure practical importance.

### Compare two independent means

For the two independent groups defined earlier,
the corresponding Welch test is:

```{r}
two_mean_test(group1, group2)
```

This test examines whether the population mean difference
is zero. Its default uses Welch's approximate degrees
of freedom rather than assuming equal variances.
A non-significant result does not establish that the
population means are equal.

For matched observations, use `paired_mean_test()` instead.
Pairing must follow the data collection design.

## Fit a linear model

R's built-in `mtcars` data provide an executable illustration. The example does
not establish causal effects or demonstrate that the model assumptions hold.

```{r}
model <- ols_fit(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
ols_coef_ci(model)
ols_predict_ci(model, data.frame(wt = 3, hp = 150), interval = "confidence")
ols_predict_ci(model, data.frame(wt = 3, hp = 150), interval = "prediction")
```

A confidence interval concerns the mean response at those predictor values.
A prediction interval concerns a future individual response. These are classical
OLS calculations, not heteroscedasticity-robust or clustered inference. Their
assumptions require review for the intended application.

## Plan a sample size

```{r}
sample_size_mean(delta = 0.5, sd = 1, power = 0.8)
```

This plans a one-sample t test to detect a difference of 0.5 units under a
normal-model SD of 1. It rounds the sample size up and reports achieved model-based
power. For `type = "two.sample"`, the returned size is **per group**, with equal
sizes and variances assumed. For `type = "paired"`, `sd` is the SD of pair differences.

## Find all functions and help

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bambagana_catalog()
sort(getNamespaceExports("bambaganaCI"))
help(package = "bambaganaCI")
help("proportion_ci", package = "bambaganaCI")
example("proportion_ci", package = "bambaganaCI")
vignette("getting-started", package = "bambaganaCI")
```

Missing and infinite observations are rejected rather than silently dropped.
Choose how to handle missingness before calling the package and record that choice.
Read warnings: a function returning an interval is not proof of reliable coverage.


<!-- BEGIN BAMBAGANA SIMPLE INPUT GUIDE -->

## Running an analysis with `bambagana()`

The `bambagana()` interface is designed for common analyses
without requiring users to memorize individual function names.

```{r bambagana-simple-input-guide}
library(bambaganaCI)

scores <- c(65, 72, 68, 75, 70, 78, 74, 69, 73, 76)

# Mean confidence interval
bambagana("mean", scores)

# Test the hypothesis that the population mean equals 70
bambagana("test mean", scores, mu = 70)

# Proportion: successes first, trials second
bambagana("proportion", c(65, 100))

# Compare independent proportions
bambagana("compare proportions", c(65, 100), c(45, 100))
```

The same function can compare means or evaluate paired data:

```{r bambagana-group-examples}
group_A <- c(65, 72, 68, 75, 70, 78, 74, 69, 73, 76)
group_B <- c(71, 79, 75, 82, 77, 85, 80, 74, 78, 81)

bambagana("compare means", group_A, group_B)
bambagana("test two means", group_A, group_B)
```

The statistical result can be saved and reused:

```{r bambagana-result-access}
result <- bambagana("mean", scores, display = FALSE)

result$estimate
result$lower
result$upper
```

By default, `bambagana()` displays the analysis in the console.
Set `display = FALSE` to retrieve the result without displaying it.

For additional analyses and examples, run:

```r
bambagana("methods")
```

Individual functions remain available for direct statistical work.
The simplified interface does not change their computations.


### Descriptive statistics and interpretation

```{r bambagana-descriptive-output}
bambagana("describe", scores)
```

The output is formatted for reading while the underlying data-frame result remains available for further analysis. Proportion intervals preserve their percentage units, and two-sample tests distinguish sample differences from population-level evidence.

<!-- END BAMBAGANA SIMPLE INPUT GUIDE -->



## Accessing the complete statistical library

The simplified interface supports all exported statistical functions through readable command names.

```{r full-bambagana-catalog}
functions <- bambagana("all functions", display = FALSE)
head(functions)
```

The table provides command names and corresponding function signatures. Results retain their original statistical structure.
